attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack essay, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'so far as I know' and the 'latest models' scope, and lists all six limitations. 'So far as I know' qualifies his knowledge, not the probability of the claim, so it stays a firm observation.

contract.note: The November 2025 window, the bar of reliability across tasks rather than isolated errors, and the rule that specialist models must be named and compared on matched tasks are ordinary, even-handed readings. Assessing each component separately is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure, dated within the window, that Opus 4.5 browser use still carries meaningful prompt-injection risk. It supports the 'hard to control' part only, and only under adversarial attack.
Dated October 2025, before the window, and about GPT-5 only. It shows mixed results against domain-tuned baselines and cannot settle the claim about the latest models.

November testing in which Gemini 3 Pro beat specialized clinical tools on MedQA. This cuts against the specialist part, but the comparators are applications, not domain-specific models, so it is not decisive.

reviews.rationale: Only the control part has evidence from the window, and it is the company's own adversarial result. Nothing in the packet tests reasoning, ordinary tool use, hallucination or alignment for November models. The specialist comparison is unsettled: e6 points the other way, but its comparators do not match the claim. The packet does not settle the claim as a whole.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'hundreds of models' scope and the universal 'always'. The framing is rhetorical, but it carries an empirical claim that failure modes recur.

contract.note: Reading the claim as about recurring categories of failure, not identical error rates, is a fair, ordinary reading. Keeping 'hundreds' and 'always' follows his own wording.

evidence.note: HalluLens (April 2025) finds hallucination recurring across 13 models from several families. That supports a narrow recurrence claim only: one failure category and far fewer than hundreds of models.

reviews.rationale: The packet has one benchmark covering 13 models and one failure category. It cannot establish that the listed failure modes persisted across hundreds of models over three years. The packet also has no evidence that any model resolved them. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own critique of Huang's remarks on the investor call, in his own voice. The Huang quotation is the target of the claim, not the claim itself.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully gives both parts: the remarks don't show that compute brings AGI, and Huang conflates exponential costs with exponential benefits. It is an assessment of an argument, testable only against the transcript.

contract.note: Judging the actual remarks, not whether AGI will come, is fair. Whether 'conflating' means an explicit equivalence or an implied one is an interpretation Marcus did not supply, and the result turns on it.

evidence.note: The transcript of the November 19 call. Huang ties more compute to more intelligence and calls compute needs exponential, but never mentions AGI and states no explicit equivalence between costs and benefits. Whether that is a conflation is a matter of interpretation.

reviews.rationale: The first part holds trivially: the remarks offer no case that compute brings AGI, and Huang never raises AGI. The conflation charge depends on how one reads 'post-training is scaling exponentially' next to 'the smarter it is'. The transcript neither clearly shows nor refutes a conflation, so the claim as a whole is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own essay.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'corporate end users' and 'must have imagined'. It compares returns with unspecified expectations held by unnamed people.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to substitute a particular survey for 'many people', since that would add a commitment Marcus never made. Without a group and an expected return to compare against, the claim cannot be tested.

reviews.rationale: The claim measures returns against what 'many people must have imagined' and names no group, expected return, metric or time horizon. Any test would have to pick a baseline Marcus did not give. It is too vague to score. The case is not broken; the claim simply cannot be scored.
